stream.title: Winchester Fall Town Meeting Session 1, Nov. 5, 2026

updates.title: Capital vice chair seeks $410,000 for school HVAC and controls design
updates.dek: Ambrose pipes have failed, and some upper floors run extremely hot
updates.body:
Capital Planning Committee Vice Chair Stefanie Mnayarji presented Article 10, which asks for $410,000 from the Building Stabilization Fund for three design and study projects. Frattaroli noted that Articles 8 and 9 were already approved on the consent agenda.

Mnayarji said the goal is to pay for planning now so the town isn't “making expensive emergency decisions tomorrow.”

## The three projects
• Ambrose School HVAC, $300,000: The heating system dates to the school's 2005 opening. Failures in the heating water pipes have disrupted heating and school operations. The design would weigh repair against replacement, including air conditioning and energy-efficiency and carbon-reduction options. The town would look for grants, such as Climate Leaders and the state's Accelerated Repair Program, and try to limit disruption to students and staff.
• Building management systems, $60,000: The systems act as “mission control” for heating, cooling and other building equipment. Winchester pioneered the technology about 20 years ago, Mnayarji said, but some of it is now obsolete and nearing the end of its manufacturer's warranty and support. The design would cover newer and older buildings and fit into future construction.
• McCall and Vinson-Owen schools, $50,000: A feasibility study and preliminary design for HVAC improvements. Some cooling equipment at Vinson-Owen is near the end of its life, and upper-level classrooms at both schools lack air conditioning. “It is not uncommon for the third floor to reach three digit temperatures,” she said.

updates.title: Capital Planning chair outlines $4.8 million in projects as Article 7 passes
updates.dek: Five-year requests outrun funding by $21 million
updates.body:
Capital Planning Committee Chair Enzo Rascionato presented the committee's report, and Town Meeting passed Article 7. The report describes $4.8 million in spending across 17 projects:
• $2.5 million from the Capital Stabilization Fund.
• $1.5 million from the Building Stabilization Fund.
• $140,000 for the cemetery.
• $700,000 for water and sewer.

## How the articles are organized
Articles 10 and 11 cover building, HVAC and field projects. Articles 12 and 13, vehicles and streets, draw on the Capital Stabilization Fund. Article 14 combines cemetery and water and sewer projects. Article 15, Lincoln School concrete repairs, is sponsored by the town manager and would be paid from the Building Stabilization Fund. Rascionato said the committee reviewed, ranked and recommended it.

## The future costs
Eight of the projects are designs, studies and early phases, and Rascionato said they will lead to about $8 million more in future years. That is an estimate, he said, and could be higher or lower. The biggest are the Ambrose School HVAC project, districtwide building controls and shoring work at Mystic School.

“When you're voting one and a half you're really voting almost 10,” he said, which is why the five-year plan matters.

## The five-year gap
Departments requested $79 million over five years, Rascionato said. Backing out $16 million for water and sewer projects, which have separate funding, leaves $63 million. About $42 million in funding is expected from the two stabilization funds and a small assumption for community preservation money, leaving a gap of about $21 million. He put it as $1.50 in requests for every $1 in funding.

“It's not the Titanic slide you might have seen in the past, but it ain't a Carnival cruise either,” he said.

## Town Hall
Six projects account for about $29 million of the requests, and Rascionato said they are too big to pay for in cash. The biggest is Town Hall, which has been in the queue for three or four years and the committee's top-ranked project for roughly three years running. Spring Town Meeting paid for an assessment. He said he expects to return next spring with a clearer scope and funding options, and hopes to work with the town manager, Select Board and the Winchester Committee for Community Preservation.

“That's going to take a village to fund,” he said.

updates.title: Town Meeting passes all three zoning articles by voice vote
updates.dek: Moderator reminded members each needed a two-thirds majority
updates.body:
Town Meeting approved Articles 4, 5 and 6, the Planning Board's zoning bylaw changes, by voice vote. Moderator Philip Frattaroli reminded members that each needed a two-thirds majority. No clicker counts were taken.

• Article 4, lot width: Frattaroli declared a two-thirds majority. He did not say it was unanimous.
• Article 5, striking the downtown review subcommittee: carried unanimously.
• Article 6, streamlining Zoning Board of Appeals procedures: carried unanimously.

updates.title: Planning Board presents three zoning articles together
updates.dek: Lot width, design review and permit steps get streamlined
updates.body:
Planning Board Chair Jack LeMenager presented Articles 4, 5 and 6 together. All three are minor zoning bylaw changes. Moderator Philip Frattaroli then asked Select Board Chair Anthea Brady for the board's recommendation. All three later passed; see the next update.

## Article 4: lot width
Planning Board member Brian Vernaglia presented it. One change would let a conforming addition go ahead by right on a lot that is too narrow, as already allowed when a lot's area or frontage falls short. The other would lower the minimum lot width in the RDA district from 120 feet to 100 feet to match its frontage rule. Vernaglia said a full rewrite of the bylaw section on pre-existing nonconforming structures could come as early as spring 2027.

“I think he got his Ph.D. in 3.5, didn't you?” LeMenager joked about Vernaglia's expertise in that section.

## Article 5: downtown design review
The article would strike the Center Business District Review Subcommittee, created in the 2015 downtown bylaw. LeMenager said applicants have gone through four reviews instead of the intended two, because the Design Review Committee and Historical Commission also review projects independently. Both voted unanimously last month to support the change. The Design Review Committee asked to stay involved in later design phases.

## Article 6: Zoning Board of Appeals process
The article would drop an old requirement for up to 16 paper copies of plans, extend the time to send materials to advisory boards from three days to five, and combine site plan review and a special permit into one hearing and one decision.

updates.title: Planning Board chair reports 194 new housing units in the works
updates.dek: Report is received and filed; three zoning articles are next
updates.body:
Planning Board Chair Jack LeMenager, a Precinct 6 Town Meeting member, reported on the board's work since the spring meeting. The board has held 13 meetings and handled four main projects, and he highlighted three older ones that are moving forward. Members then voted to receive and file the report; the motion carried with no opposition heard.

## Four projects since spring
• 972 Main St., the former Meineke Muffler site, is under construction plans for a building with 13 rental units, one of them affordable, one ground-floor commercial unit and 15 below-grade parking spaces. The Historical Commission cleared demolition last month. A design subcommittee will settle details left open in the special permit, including the fourth floor and window designs, and construction is expected to take about 18 months.
• 1016 Mount Vernon St. won approval Oct. 6 for a third floor that adds four downtown rentals. An elevator will make all nine units accessible.
• 910 Main St., at Canal Street, is still being negotiated. The plan is three floors with about 14 rentals, 14 or more underground spaces and one or two commercial spaces. LeMenager hopes to settle remaining details by the end of the year or early next year.

## Three older projects
• The friendly 40B on Cross Street is nine rental townhouses and is nearly built. LeMenager corrected himself during the meeting: it has two affordable units, not one.
• 25 Waterfield, beside the train station, could break ground as soon as January. It would have 56 rentals, 40 of them affordable, and 119 parking spaces, 71 of them public.
• The Washington and Swanton streets project is finishing its contract language. LeMenager expects ground to be broken in mid-2027 for 64 rentals, 16 of them affordable, and 104 parking spaces.

Together, the seven projects add about 194 housing units, 63 of them affordable, he said. A total of 111 count toward the state's subsidized housing inventory, which he said would bring Winchester to about 6.29 percent, a figure he credited to the town planner. “But don't quote me,” he said.

## What's next
The board plans more bylaw changes in the spring and will start work on the next master plan. LeMenager said a statewide ballot question that would have forced major zoning rewrites appeared headed for defeat as of this afternoon. The board meets the first Tuesday of each month at 7 p.m. in the Select Board Room and is broadcast on WinCAM.

updates.title: Town Meeting reconvenes as new members are sworn in
updates.dek: Moderator swears in new members, then turns to Article 2
updates.body:
Town Meeting reconvened after the precinct meetings, and Moderator Philip Frattaroli administered the oath of office to the new Town Meeting members. “Congratulations, you all! Welcome to the party,” he told them.

Members' clickers were being programmed for electronic voting as the meeting moved to Article 2, the Planning Board report.

updates.title: Shout-out to WinCAM's Allan Eyden for terrific Town Meeting recaps
updates.dek: Recess briefing walks viewers through consent agenda
updates.body: While members met by precinct, WinCAM's Allan Eyden gave viewers a recap of the night so far, including the opening, the three members honored and the consent agenda article by article. Thank you, Allan, for the terrific recaps. Eyden said a wrap-up of tonight's session will follow when the meeting ends.

updates.title: Consent agenda, article by article: 12 pass, one postponed, one pulled
updates.dek: Plain-English rundown of what members approved without debate
updates.body:
Town Meeting approved the consent agenda without debate. Here is what each article does, using the amounts printed in the motion book.

• Article 3: Housekeeping about seats of members who miss too many sessions. The motion book calls for indefinite postponement, so no seats were declared vacant.
• Article 8: Returns $18,277.30 in unspent capital money to the capital stabilization fund and $8,587.24 to cemetery perpetual care.
• Article 9: Rescinds $1.15 million in 2021 borrowing authority for Muraco School repairs that was not needed.
• Article 16: Adjusts fiscal 2027 budgets approved in the spring, including $193,250 for debt interest.
• Article 17: Adds $62,664 to water and sewer expenses.
• Article 18: Replaces $343,000 of estimated recreation receipts with the department's retained earnings.
• Article 20: Spends $19,000 from the parking meter fund on the Town Center and Wedgemere parking lots.
• Article 21: Moves $148,000 of free cash into the health insurance stabilization fund.
• Article 22: Appropriates about $225,650 from the cable access fund, including $45,000 for capital needs.
• Article 27: Raises dog license fees by $10, to $30 for most dogs and $25 for spayed or neutered dogs.
• Article 28: Creates a school transportation revolving fund.
• Articles 31 and 32: Accept state laws that let the town place liens for unpaid water and sewer bills.

Moderator Philip Frattaroli pulled Article 19, a $350,000 free cash transfer toward retiree health costs, so members will debate it separately.

updates.title: Town Meeting accepts Article 1 reports
updates.dek: Reports from Select Board, schools and others came first
updates.body: Town Meeting members voted to pass Article 1, which accepts the reports of town officials, boards, committees and commissions. Members heard from the Select Board, the Finance Committee, the town manager, the Long Range Financial Planning Committee and the school superintendent and School Committee chair before the vote. The motion carried on a voice vote.

updates.title: School leaders urge operating override as Muraco advances
updates.dek: Chair says last spring's cuts eliminated 32.5 positions

images.alt: A man in a dark suit speaks from a podium at the right side of a school auditorium while a large screen on stage shows a slide titled Tonight's roadmap.
images.caption: Superintendent Frank Hackett presents the district's Article 1 report Thursday.

images.alt: A man in glasses and a dark suit speaks from a podium at the right side of a school auditorium while a large screen on stage shows a slide titled Our FY2028 budget process is well underway.
images.caption: School Committee Chair Timothy Matthews presents the FY2028 budget slide Thursday.

updates.body:
Superintendent Frank Hackett and School Committee Chair Timothy Matthews gave the Winchester Public Schools report. They said the district is performing well but still absorbing last spring's cuts, and the committee believes an operating override is urgently needed.

## District update
Hackett said the district is in full implementation of a new literacy curriculum funded by Town Meeting last year. Thirty seniors from the class of 2026 now play collegiate sports, almost 10 percent of the class. Winchester High School had four National Merit finalists.

About 90 percent of the district's budget goes to personnel, he said, and about 90 percent of personnel belong to a union. Enrollment has fallen over 10 years and is now relatively flat, but students' needs have grown.

A survey of parents, staff and students identified five priorities, including class size, fee affordability and course access. Elementary parents most often cited math interventionists, and Hackett said higher fees keep some students off athletic teams.

## The cuts and the budget
Matthews said the failed operating override forced the district to cut $3.2 million from its original budget projection and eliminate 32.5 full-time positions. Athletic fees rose 68 percent and transportation fees 10 percent, and the district drained its special education reserve. Nine more students needed out-of-district placements, and state transportation costs jumped.

The district concluded agreements with all five Winchester Education Association bargaining units. It began its fiscal 2028 budget process early, and the committee held a workshop on the survey results this past week.

“Instead of entering a process of managed decline,” Matthews said, the committee believes “an operating override is urgently needed to provide stable funding that allows all of Winchester students to grow and to succeed.”

## Muraco and the committee's articles
Matthews said the Massachusetts School Building Authority board voted unanimously last month to accept Muraco Elementary School into its feasibility phase. It was one of the first three schools in its cohort accepted. The district will next hire a designer and an owner's project manager, then compare repairing, renovating and expanding, or replacing the building. The district has launched a Muraco website for updates.

The state board's invitation came Oct. 28, according to Winchester News. Muraco entered the state's eligibility period in December 2025, after the district's fourth request. Winchester applied for both Lynch and Muraco in 2017, 2018 and 2019, and the state chose Lynch. Spring Town Meeting approved a $1.5 million study appropriation. At Winchester's 32.47 percent reimbursement rate, the town would get back about $487,000 and pay about $1.01 million, depending on what the state deems eligible.

The earliest the state could approve a project scope and budget is after July 1, 2028. If the schedule holds, a new or renovated Muraco would open for the 2030-31 school year.

The one-story building at 33 Bates Road dates to the 1960s. Enrollment has fallen from 404 students in 2016-17 to 286 at the end of August. The district's 2025 application cited nearly 200 single-pane windows about 60 years old and uninsulated exterior walls. “Cold students cannot learn well,” the district wrote.

The School Committee has three articles. One passed on the consent agenda. Matthews said the committee will return for Article 29, replenishing the special education reserve, and Article 30, next steps for the Sanborn Carriage House. Questions can go to schoolcommittee@winchesterps.org.
updates.sourceLabel: Winchester News on Muraco's feasibility study

updates.title: Long-range finance panel studies how other towns plan budgets
updates.dek: Select Board member Prior says group is 'not the override accelerator committee'
updates.body:
Select Board member Michelle Prior updated Town Meeting on the Long Range Financial Planning Committee, which is building a shared financial framework for the town. The committee is looking at revenue and expense targets, an operating reserve forecast, how to split money between general stabilization and free cash, and a multi-year plan.

## What it is studying
Prior said other AAA-rated communities have done this for years. Brookline's town-school partnership dates to 1995, Arlington's to 2005 and Shrewsbury's to 2010. The committee is talking with those towns and hearing ideas that include:
• Setting minimums for capital spending.
• Using a predictable share of free cash in the budget; some towns use up to half.
• Setting year-over-year spending targets.
• Taking shared costs such as capital, health insurance and pensions off the top of revenue and splitting what is left.
• Making regular deposits into the stabilization fund. Winchester made its first in 15 years last spring, she said.
• Creating a process for positive and negative surprises.

## The problem
Winchester has a structural deficit, Prior said. The town expected a $5 million gap at the spring meeting and ended up needing $3.4 million of free cash to balance the budget. She said the gap is larger heading into next year. Capital needs persist, she said, and there is still no solution for Town Hall.

## Next steps
The committee plans to agree on the facts, identify outcomes, explore efficiencies, discuss trade-offs and move from targets to rules, such as a growth target or a rule to spend only the revenue left after shared expenses.

“Good relationships matter,” Prior said. “Durable, enforceable policies might just matter more.”

She said officials in Andover told the committee their budget process is boring. “That sounds terrific to me,” Prior said.

“We are not the override accelerator committee,” she said. “We are here to take the long view.”

updates.title: Senior: New fees add revenue, but costs and delays persist
updates.dek: Town manager also cites hiring holds, software upgrades and a staff 'fun committee'
updates.body:
Town Manager Christopher Senior told Town Meeting that the town is raising revenue and holding down costs in small steps, though inflation, tariffs and borrowing costs keep pressure on the budget.

## Revenue
Downtown parking tags rose from $10 to $50 a year, and Senior said parking revenue is up $40,000 so far over last year as the town manages the machines more actively. The Mystic School's new lease, which includes energy payments, brings in about $16,000 more. Building and zoning fees are running 16 percent above what the old fee schedule would have produced from April to October, he said.

“None of these by themselves changes the needle,” Senior said. “But I want you to understand that we're looking at all of these things.”

## Costs and efficiency
Senior said he has asked department heads to hold some open positions, including delaying hires until winter in one department. He is also pushing to modernize paperwork. Police are working toward electronic ticketing devices, and the town plans to end paper time sheets. Article 33, the software funding request, would put licensing and permitting on one town-wide platform; it is expected later in the meeting.

The town's pension is about to be paid off, he said, and more money is going into the OPEB reserve for retiree health care. Health care costs, building-material prices and interest rates remain challenges. Borrowing costs about 5 percent now, up from about 3 percent. Steel prices have made one solar parking-lot project uneconomical, he said.

“It shouldn't take two years to get a fire truck,” Senior said.

## Staff
Senior said he meets every new hire, including two 21-year-old Winchester High School graduates who interned with the fire department and are now joining it. A compensation and classification study is wrapping up. He also described a staff “fun committee” that organized a pumpkin-carving event, with an employee recognition event planned in a few weeks.

“A staff that works well together and has fun together really works better together,” he said.

image.alt: A man in a suit speaks from a podium at the right side of a school auditorium while a large screen on stage shows a group photo of staff seated around a long table.
image.caption: Town Manager Christopher Senior gives his Article 1 report Thursday as a staff photo appears on screen.

updates.title: Brady cites health insurance, inflation as budget pressures
updates.dek: Select Board chair also notes culvert work and new crossing beacons
updates.body:
Select Board Chair Anthea Brady opened the Article 1 reports with a brief update on town projects, then turned to budget pressures. The board has installed several rapid flashing beacons at pedestrian crossings around town, and work on the Muraco School culvert began in earnest late this summer. Brady said she hopes it will be largely finished by early next year.

## Budget pressures
Health insurance remains a major cost driver, Brady said, and the year-to-year increases are hard to predict. Construction-material inflation, higher energy costs and tariffs add to the strain. The town also has to offer competitive pay to keep staff, and it carries long-term liabilities such as retiree health care, known as OPEB.

“It is often a very large increase that we need to manage,” Brady said of health insurance.

## Managing costs
The board reviewed fees in other towns with department heads and updated several of Winchester's, including parking fees. Some had not changed in more than 10 years, Brady said. The board is also working on efficiencies, liabilities and staff retention.

She asked members to support the articles the Select Board is presenting tonight.

updates.title: Moderator congratulates new senators, then clears consent agenda
updates.dek: Seven preliminary motions pass before first town report
updates.body:
Moderator Philip Frattaroli congratulated Uyterhoeven and Lipper-Garabedian, along with Rep. Michael Day, who was re-elected. He also thanked Sen. Jason Lewis, a Winchester resident who is retiring from the Senate.

Frattaroli said it will be the first time in nearly 95 years that no Winchester resident serves in the General Court. “If there's any ambitious, young, dynamic, social media conscious politicians in the room who'd like to represent the town, the call goes out,” he said.

## Preliminary motions
Members approved seven preliminary motions by voice vote. They let town officials who are not Town Meeting members and Finance Committee members sit at the front of the auditorium, and they set later sessions for Mondays and Thursdays at 7 p.m. They also make spending contingent on Proposition 2½ and allow cable television coverage.

## Consent agenda
Frattaroli pulled Article 19, the retiree benefits reserve transfer, from the consent agenda, citing “the discussion of the select board meeting on Monday and elsewhere.” Members then approved the rest unanimously without debate: Articles 3, 8, 9, 16 through 18, 20 through 22, 27, 28, 31 and 32.

Debate begins with Article 1, reports of town officials and boards, starting with Select Board Chair Anthea Brady.

updates.title: Town Meeting honors Vincent Dixon, Janice Dolan and Eric Shediac
updates.dek: Moderator leads silence for three who died and salutes retiring Sen. Lewis
updates.body:
Moderator Philip Frattaroli led a moment of silence for three Town Meeting members who have died since the spring meeting, naming Vincent Dixon, Janice Dolan and Eric Shediac.

Frattaroli also honored outgoing Sen. Jason Lewis, a member of Town Meeting who is retiring from the state Senate. He joked that he hopes Lewis will use his free time to attend more meetings.

## Vincent Dixon
Dixon, a historian, tour guide and perennial candidate, died July 11 at Tufts Medical Center in Boston at age 74. He had lived in Winchester for 13 years and won a Precinct 3 Town Meeting seat in 2025 with 178 votes.

He grew up in Allston and lived in Cambridge for many years, where he founded Cambridge Advantage, a company that led tours on history, transportation, real estate and city government. He also started Harvard Yard tours, which Harvard later took over. In Winchester, he led Town Day trolley tours and served on the Finance Committee from 2015 to 2019.

Dixon hosted “The Vince Dixon Show of History, Current Events, and the Rule of Law” on WinCAM and gave frequent talks for the Winchester Historical Society. His spring 2019 talk on the town's parks and beaches filled a room at Sanborn House. He was preparing a talk on the nation's 250th anniversary when he was hospitalized.

A Winchester News tally found at least 18 bids for elected office over about 35 years, including races for the Massachusetts Senate, Middlesex County sheriff, Cambridge City Council, the Governor's Council and, repeatedly, the Winchester Select Board. He finished fourth of four for two Select Board seats in 2024.

He also had legislation filed on his behalf in the General Court over several sessions, much of it through Sen. Jason Lewis and Rep. Michael Day. None became law.

Frattaroli recalled joking at the spring meeting that Dixon had “a reputation for being long-winded.” He said Dixon also had a reputation for being “impeccably informed.”

“Civics is at once relatively simple, and its details and how they interact can be complex,” Dixon said, according to the Winchester News profile.

Emilieanne Koehnlein, his partner of 14 years, told Winchester News he believed no one should run unopposed. “I am not going to let his work die,” she said of his legacy.

Select Board Chair Anthea Brady called him “a bit of a staple in our Winchester government scene.”

## Janice Dolan
Frattaroli said Dolan, a Precinct 5 member for 50 years, spent 40 years teaching physical education at Winchester High School, where she coached girls tennis and field hockey. He said she taught him, too.

She also drove Meals on Wheels, he said, and the Winchester Sports Hall of Fame created the Jan Dolan Legacy Leadership Award in her honor in 2025.

## Eric Shediac
Frattaroli remembered Shediac as a Town Meeting member, a husband and father, and a volunteer coach who was active in the community.

updates.title: Moderator opens Fall Town Meeting after quorum is confirmed
updates.dek: Zoning and capital planning top Frattaroli's agenda for the night
updates.body:
Moderator Philip Frattaroli opened the meeting after the town clerk confirmed a quorum. A Girl Scout color guard presented the colors, and a Brownie Girl Scout named Ella led the Pledge of Allegiance.

Frattaroli said members will hear from boards and committees, then break for precinct meetings as the bylaws require. Tonight's business is mainly zoning, he said, and members hope to finish the capital planning report and its related articles.

Members stood for a moment of silence for three members who have died since the spring meeting.

Frattaroli briefly stumbled over the meeting's year. “It's been a long week,” he said.

image.alt: A projection screen on a school auditorium stage shows the town seal and the words Fall Town Meeting 2026, with a podium and clerk's table on the stage and officials seated at a table in the foreground.
image.caption: Fall Town Meeting opens Thursday at Winchester High School.

updates.title: Senator-elect Uyterhoeven introduces herself to Town Meeting
updates.dek: Second Middlesex winner pledges openness and promotes a weekly newsletter
updates.body:
State Rep. Erika Uyterhoeven, who won the Second Middlesex Senate seat unopposed Tuesday, introduced herself to Town Meeting members. The seat covers Winchester Precincts 4, 5, 6 and 7, and she takes office in January. Results are unofficial. Kate Lipper-Garabedian, a Melrose Democrat, also won her Senate seat unopposed Tuesday; the Fifth Middlesex seat covers Winchester Precincts 1, 2, 3 and 8.

She said she publishes a weekly newsletter on State House business; her most recent issue covered the nine statewide ballot questions.

“One of my grounding principles running for office is more transparency and more accessibility to state government,” Uyterhoeven said.

She said the issues Town Meeting handles overlap with her work. “Something I'm really passionate about is really fighting to lower the cost of living, ensure that we're funding our schools,” she said. “All things that I know you all deal with in town meeting, you know, intersects with what we do in the state house.”

image.alt: A woman in a plaid blazer speaks into a microphone from a railing at the side of a school auditorium while Town Meeting members seated in red chairs look on.
image.caption: State Rep. Erika Uyterhoeven speaks to Town Meeting members Thursday.

updates.title: Fall Town Meeting opens tonight: What’s on the floor

image.alt: Town Meeting members seated in a school auditorium facing the stage, where officials sit at tables beneath a projected slide.
image.caption: Winchester Town Meeting in session at a previous meeting.

updates.body:
Town Meeting begins tonight at 7 p.m. at Winchester High School. Members will work through 45 articles over as many as four nights: Nov. 5, 9 and 12, with Nov. 16 in reserve.

## The big picture
Most of the warrant is about money, and most of it is routine. The biggest piece is about $4.8 million in capital requests, including a $1.1 million fire engine, road and sidewalk work and $900,000 for walkways and stairs at Lincoln School.

The rest covers Community Preservation projects; zoning and land deals; and bylaw changes ranging from dog license fees to sidewalk snow removal.

## What to watch
• Forest Ridge (Article 26): A proposed eminent domain taking of about 13 acres for conservation, with a $2.85 million appraisal ceiling in the draft motion.
• Citizen petitions (Articles 39–43): Rezonings at 114 Church St. and 18 Raymond Place; a new home lot at the Ledges; and a call for separate override votes. The Church Street petitioner has said they won’t pursue it this fall.
• Sanborn Carriage House (Article 30): A $50,000 study, and the only article the Select Board opposes.
• Special education reserve (Article 29): $400,000, backed 3-1 by the Select Board.

## Where things stand
The Select Board has backed 18 articles and opposed one. Winchester News has not confirmed its position on the other 26. Every vote is still ahead, and we’ll post results here as they happen.
updates.dek: Members face 45 articles, from a Forest Ridge land taking to dog license fees
